questions.q: Which statement best defines cloud computing?
o: Delivering computing services such as servers, storage and databases over the internet, on demand
Installing every application on local office computers
Connecting two offices with a private cable
Buying a fixed amount of hardware every five years
questions.e: Cloud computing is on-demand delivery of computing resources over the internet, usually with pay-as-you-go pricing.
questions.af: Like switching on a tap: you do not dig a well, you open the tap and pay for the water you use.

questions.q: A company stops buying servers upfront and instead pays a monthly bill for the compute it uses. Which change is this?
questions.e: Cloud turns large upfront capital expenses (CapEx) into ongoing operational expenses (OpEx).
questions.af: A Nairobi startup no longer saves KES 2 million for a server. It pays monthly, like buying airtime instead of a phone line.

questions.q: A bank keeps customer records in its own datacenter but runs a public-facing app in Azure, with the two connected. Which cloud model is this?
questions.e: Hybrid cloud combines private or on-premises infrastructure with a public cloud so workloads sit where they fit best.
questions.af: Keeping your savings in the bank vault while using mobile money for daily payments.

questions.q: A ministry's rules say sensitive records must stay on hardware that the ministry owns and controls. Which model fits best?
questions.e: A private cloud is used by a single organisation and can sit in its own datacenter. The trade-off is that the organisation maintains the hardware.
questions.af: A family kitchen where only your household cooks, rather than a shared community kitchen.

questions.q: Which pricing idea means you are billed only for what you actually use, with no upfront cost?
questions.e: In the consumption-based model you pay per use (per minute, per GB, per execution) and stop paying when you stop using.
questions.af: Pay-as-you-go electricity tokens: you only pay for the units you burn.

questions.q: A workload will run 24/7 for three years. Which pricing approach usually gives a lower price than pay-as-you-go, in return for a commitment?
questions.e: Azure Reservations give a discount when you commit to a 1- or 3-year term for steady workloads. Pay-as-you-go suits unpredictable usage.
questions.af: A monthly bus pass is cheaper than single tickets if you travel the same route every day.

questions.q: A team wants code to run only when an event occurs, with no servers to manage, and pay only per execution. Which approach fits?
questions.e: Serverless (for example Azure Functions) runs code on demand. Azure manages the servers and bills by execution and resources used.
questions.af: A boda-boda: you pay per trip instead of owning and maintaining the motorbike.

questions.q: Under the shared responsibility model, which item is always the customer's responsibility, whatever the service type?
o: Information and data, and who can access it
questions.e: Microsoft always handles the physical datacenter, hosts and network. Customers always own their data, identities and access decisions.
questions.af: A landlord secures the building, but you decide who you give a key to.

questions.q: Large cloud providers can offer lower prices per unit than most companies could manage alone. Which benefit is this?
questions.e: Economies of scale: massive purchasing power and shared infrastructure lower the cost per unit passed on to customers.
questions.af: Buying maize flour by the sack at the depot is cheaper per kilo than buying small packets.

questions.q: A retailer's site gets 20 times the traffic on Black Friday, then returns to normal. Which benefit lets resources grow and shrink to match this?
questions.e: Elasticity is the ability to scale resources out and in as demand changes, so you pay for peaks only while they last.
questions.af: Like extra matatus put on the road for the Friday rush and taken off when it ends.

questions.q: Adding more VM instances to handle load is an example of which kind of scaling?
questions.e: Horizontal scaling adds instances. Vertical scaling makes one instance bigger (more CPU or RAM).
questions.af: Opening more checkout lanes at a supermarket rather than making one cashier work faster.

questions.q: Which statement about availability SLAs is correct?
o: SLAs only apply to on-premises systems
questions.e: An SLA states an uptime target. Higher percentages mean less permitted downtime, but nothing guarantees zero downtime.
questions.af: A courier promising 99.99% on-time delivery is stricter than one promising 99.9%.

questions.q: Which cloud benefit describes a system recovering from failures and continuing to work?
questions.e: Reliability (and fault tolerance) is the ability to recover from failures and keep serving users, helped by redundancy across zones and regions.
questions.af: A generator that starts during load-shedding so the shop keeps selling.

questions.q: Autoscaling and load balancing keep performance steady, and cost tools help forecast spend. Which benefit is this?
questions.e: Predictability covers both performance (autoscale, load balancing) and cost (forecasting and budgeting tools).
questions.af: Knowing your monthly airtime budget and that calls will connect even at peak hours.

questions.q: Which is a security and governance benefit of using the cloud?
o: Built-in tools and compliance certifications you can apply across resources
You never need to manage identities
questions.e: Cloud platforms provide threat protection, policy enforcement and compliance offerings. You still configure and govern your own resources.
questions.af: A shopping mall with guards and CCTV already installed; you still lock your own shop.

questions.q: A team deploys identical environments from templates and monitors them with the CLI and portal. Which benefit is this?
questions.e: Manageability covers management of the cloud (autoscaling, templates, monitoring) and management in the cloud (portal, CLI, APIs).
questions.af: A franchise manual that lets every branch run the same way.

questions.q: In an IaaS virtual machine, who is responsible for patching the guest operating system?
questions.e: With IaaS, Microsoft runs hosts, network and datacenter. The customer manages the OS, apps and data on the VM.
questions.af: Renting an empty shop: the landlord fixes the building, but you stock and clean the shop yourself.

questions.q: Which service type lets developers deploy code without managing the operating system, but still control their application?
questions.e: PaaS provides a managed platform (OS, runtime, patching). You manage your application and data. Azure App Service is an example.
questions.af: A stall in a managed market hall: power, security and cleaning are provided; you just sell.

questions.q: A company uses Microsoft 365 email. What is their responsibility?
o: Managing their data, users and access
questions.e: With SaaS the provider runs almost everything. The customer remains responsible for data, identities and access.
questions.af: Using a hosted school portal: the vendor runs it, but the school decides who gets a login.

questions.q: A company wants to move an existing on-premises application to the cloud with minimal changes and needs control of the OS. Which service type fits?
questions.e: IaaS (virtual machines) suits lift-and-shift migrations and workloads that need OS-level control.
questions.af: Moving your whole shop to a bigger building and arranging the shelves exactly as before.

questions.q: Which pairing of Azure offering and service type is correct?
questions.e: Azure VMs are IaaS, App Service is PaaS and Microsoft 365 is SaaS.
questions.af: Land (IaaS), a built shop you decorate (PaaS), a ready-to-use mobile money agent kiosk (SaaS).

questions.q: A startup wants to focus on writing its web app and avoid server maintenance entirely. Which service type is the best fit?
questions.e: PaaS removes OS and runtime maintenance so developers concentrate on code.
questions.af: A freelancer renting a fully equipped co-working desk instead of building an office.

questions.q: What is an Azure availability zone?
o: One or more physically separate datacenters inside a region with independent power, cooling and networking
questions.e: Availability zones protect against datacenter-level failure by spreading resources over separate locations in one region.
questions.af: Two separate warehouses in the same city, so a fire at one does not stop deliveries.

questions.q: What is the purpose of an Azure region pair?
o: Provide geo-redundancy and prioritised recovery between two regions in the same geography
questions.e: Regions are paired within a geography for disaster recovery, such as geo-redundant storage replication and staggered platform updates.
questions.af: A shop in Lagos with a backup stock room in another city.

questions.q: Which statement describes an Azure region?
o: A set of datacenters connected by a low-latency network within a defined area
questions.e: A region is a geographic area containing one or more datacenters networked together with low latency.
questions.af: A district office that has several buildings linked by a fast road.

questions.q: Azure Government and Azure China (operated by 21Vianet) are examples of what?
questions.e: Sovereign regions are isolated Azure instances that meet specific legal and compliance requirements for a country or sector.
questions.af: An embassy compound that follows its own rules inside a host city.

questions.q: Which statement about resource groups is true?
o: A resource can belong to several resource groups at once
A resource group is a logical container for related resources
Deleting a resource group keeps its resources
questions.e: A resource group is a logical container. Each resource lives in exactly one group, and deleting the group deletes everything inside.
questions.af: A folder on your laptop for one project. Delete the folder and the files go with it.

questions.q: Which Azure construct is the boundary for billing and access management and sits between management groups and resource groups?
questions.e: The hierarchy is management groups, subscriptions, resource groups, resources. A subscription is a billing and access boundary.
questions.af: Each department in a university having its own budget account.

questions.q: Which order lists the Azure hierarchy from broadest to narrowest scope?
o: Management group, subscription, resource group, resource
Resource group, subscription, management group, resource
Subscription, management group, resource, resource group
Resource, resource group, subscription, management group
questions.e: Management groups organise subscriptions. Policies and access assigned at a higher scope are inherited by lower scopes.
questions.af: Ministry, then department, then unit, then individual officer.

questions.q: Which compute type packages an app with its dependencies, shares the host OS kernel, and starts faster than a full VM?
questions.e: Containers are lightweight and portable because they share the host OS kernel instead of carrying a whole guest OS.
questions.af: Packed lunch boxes: everything you need is in the box, and you can carry it anywhere.

questions.q: A team wants to run and orchestrate many containers automatically. Which Azure service fits?
questions.e: AKS is a managed Kubernetes service for deploying, scaling and managing containerised applications.
questions.af: A port manager arranging hundreds of shipping containers instead of moving each by hand.

questions.q: When are Azure Virtual Machines a better fit than Azure App Service?
o: When you need full control of the operating system
When you want Microsoft to manage the runtime
When you only host a simple web page
questions.e: VMs (IaaS) give OS-level control. App Service (PaaS) hides the OS and runs your web app.
questions.af: Building your own house (full control) versus renting a furnished flat.

questions.q: Which service deploys and manages a group of identical, load-balanced VMs that can scale automatically?
questions.e: Virtual Machine Scale Sets create and manage identical VMs and can add or remove instances based on demand or a schedule.
questions.af: A taxi company that adds identical cabs when demand rises.

questions.q: What does an availability set do?
o: Spreads VMs across fault domains and update domains inside a datacenter to limit the impact of failures and maintenance
questions.e: An availability set groups VMs so that a hardware fault or planned maintenance does not take all of them down at once.
questions.af: Placing your delivery vans in different garages so one blocked road does not stop all deliveries.

questions.q: Which Azure service delivers virtualised Windows desktops and apps that users reach from any device?
questions.e: Azure Virtual Desktop is a desktop and app virtualisation service running in Azure.
questions.af: A cyber café computer you can log into from anywhere, with all your files in the same place.

questions.q: Which Azure service lets you build a private network in the cloud so resources can communicate securely?
questions.e: A VNet is your isolated network in Azure. Subnets, peering and gateways extend and connect it.
questions.af: A staff-only group chat, separate from public chats.

questions.q: You need two virtual networks to talk over private IP addresses across Microsoft's backbone. What should you use?
questions.e: VNet peering connects virtual networks so resources communicate privately using the Microsoft backbone, without a gateway or the public internet.
questions.af: A private footbridge between two buildings on the same campus.

questions.q: You need a private, dedicated connection from your office to Azure that does NOT travel over the public internet. Which service?
questions.e: ExpressRoute uses a private connection through a connectivity provider. A VPN Gateway encrypts traffic but still crosses the public internet.
questions.af: A private road straight to your warehouse versus a tunnel through the public highway.

questions.q: Which service hosts your DNS domains and resolves names using Azure infrastructure?
questions.e: Azure DNS hosts DNS domains, turning names like example.com into IP addresses.
questions.af: The phone book that turns a shop's name into its phone number.

questions.q: What does a private endpoint provide?
o: A private IP address in your virtual network for a service, so traffic stays off the public internet
A copy of your storage in another region
questions.e: A private endpoint uses Azure Private Link to bring a service into your virtual network through a private IP address.
questions.af: A staff-only side door into a shop instead of using the public entrance.

questions.q: Which Azure Storage service stores massive amounts of unstructured data such as images and video?
questions.e: Blob Storage is object storage for unstructured data like documents, media and backups.
questions.af: A photographer keeping thousands of wedding photos online.

questions.q: Which Azure Storage service provides fully managed file shares that use the SMB protocol?
questions.e: Azure Files offers managed cloud file shares accessible over SMB (and NFS).
questions.af: A shared office drive that everyone can open like a normal folder.

questions.q: Which redundancy option copies your data to a secondary region far away?
questions.e: LRS keeps copies in one datacenter, ZRS spreads them across availability zones, and GRS also replicates to a secondary region.
questions.af: Keeping a photocopy of your title deed in a different town.

questions.q: Which option protects against the failure of one datacenter by replicating across availability zones in the same region?
questions.e: Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) keeps copies in multiple availability zones of the primary region.
questions.af: Storing stock in three warehouses across the same city.

questions.q: Which blob access tier has the lowest storage cost but requires hours to rehydrate data before it can be read?
questions.e: Archive is offline storage for rarely accessed data. Hot is for frequent access, Cool and Cold for infrequent access.
questions.af: Old files in a storeroom across town: cheap to keep, slow to fetch.

questions.q: Which tool is a command-line utility for copying data to and from Azure Storage?
questions.e: AzCopy is a command-line tool for copying blobs and files. Azure Storage Explorer is the graphical alternative.
questions.af: A parcel service you call from the terminal to move many boxes at once.

questions.q: Which service keeps on-premises Windows file servers in sync with Azure Files while caching frequently used files locally?
questions.e: Azure File Sync turns a Windows Server into a fast local cache of an Azure file share.
questions.af: A branch office keeping a local copy of the head office's documents.

questions.q: Which service helps discover, assess and migrate on-premises servers, databases and apps to Azure?
questions.e: Azure Migrate is a central hub for discovering, assessing and migrating workloads to Azure.
questions.af: A moving company that first surveys your house, then plans and carries out the move.

questions.q: You must move hundreds of terabytes to Azure, and your internet link is too slow. Which option fits?
questions.e: Azure Data Box is a physical device that Microsoft ships to you; you load data onto it and ship it back for upload.
questions.af: Sending a truck of harvest to market instead of carrying it sack by sack on a bicycle.

questions.q: Which service provides cloud identity management, single sign-on and multifactor authentication for Azure and apps?
questions.e: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) is Microsoft's cloud identity and access management service.
questions.af: One staff ID card that opens every door on campus.

questions.q: Which service provides managed domain services such as domain join and LDAP without you running domain controllers?
questions.e: Entra Domain Services offers managed domain join, group policy, LDAP and Kerberos/NTLM authentication.
questions.af: Renting a ready-run school administration office instead of staffing your own.

questions.q: Which combination is an example of multifactor authentication?
o: A password plus a code from an authenticator app
A password plus the same password again
A username plus an email address
questions.e: MFA combines at least two factor types: something you know, something you have, something you are.
questions.af: An ATM needs your card (have) and your PIN (know).

questions.q: Which of these is a passwordless authentication method?
o: A password with a longer length
questions.e: Passwordless methods include Windows Hello for Business, the Microsoft Authenticator app and FIDO2 security keys.
questions.af: Opening your phone with your fingerprint instead of typing a code.

questions.q: A company wants partners from another organisation to access one app using the partners' own credentials. Which concept applies?
questions.e: External identities let guests and partners sign in with their own identities, so you do not have to create accounts for them.
questions.af: Visitors signing in at reception with their own national ID.

questions.q: Which feature requires MFA only when a user signs in from an unfamiliar location or risky device?
questions.e: Conditional Access (in Entra ID) applies access controls based on signals such as location, device and risk.
questions.af: A bank asking for extra verification when you try to log in from a new country.

questions.q: Which service grants users permissions to resources using roles at a given scope?
questions.e: Azure role-based access control assigns roles (Owner, Contributor, Reader) to identities at management group, subscription, resource group or resource scope.
questions.af: A hotel giving housekeeping a floor key but only the manager the master key.

questions.q: Which principle best describes Zero Trust?
o: Trust everything inside the corporate network
questions.e: Zero Trust verifies explicitly, uses least privilege and assumes breach. Location in the network earns no automatic trust.
questions.af: A guard who checks everyone's ID at every door, even employees.

questions.q: What is the idea behind defence in depth?
o: Using multiple layers of security so one failure does not expose everything
questions.e: Defence in depth layers protections: physical, identity, perimeter, network, compute, application and data.
questions.af: A compound with a gate, a guard dog, door locks and a safe inside.

questions.q: Which service provides security posture management and threat protection across Azure and hybrid workloads?
questions.e: Defender for Cloud assesses your security posture, gives recommendations and protects workloads against threats.
questions.af: A security firm that both checks your locks and watches the cameras.

questions.q: Which tool estimates the cost of running a planned workload in Azure before you deploy it?
questions.e: The Azure pricing calculator lets you configure services and estimate monthly costs before deployment.
questions.af: Getting a builder's quotation before you start building.

questions.q: Which is a factor that can affect Azure costs?
o: The region where a resource is deployed
The colour of the portal theme
The name of the resource group
questions.e: Resource type, usage, region, bandwidth and subscription offer type all influence cost.
questions.af: Rent for the same shop differs between Kampala city centre and a village.

questions.q: Which data movement is typically free of charge in Azure?
o: Outbound data transfer to the internet
questions.e: Data coming into Azure is generally free. Outbound transfer (egress) is charged.
questions.af: Delivering goods into the market is free; the market charges you to take them out.

questions.q: What is the main use of tags on Azure resources?
o: Organising resources and reporting cost by project or department
questions.e: Tags are name/value pairs for organisation and cost reporting. They do not grant access and are not inherited by default.
questions.af: Coloured stickers on boxes in a storeroom showing which department owns them.

questions.q: You want an alert when your monthly spend passes a set limit. What should you configure?
o: A budget with alerts in Microsoft Cost Management
questions.e: Cost Management lets you analyse spending and create budgets that trigger alerts.
questions.af: A text message when your airtime drops below KES 50.

questions.q: You want to ensure resources can only be created in approved regions. Which service enforces this?
questions.e: Azure Policy evaluates resources against rules (such as allowed locations) and can audit or deny non-compliant ones.
questions.af: A school rule that only uniform in the approved colours is allowed.

questions.q: How can you prevent an administrator from accidentally deleting a critical resource?
questions.e: Resource locks (CanNotDelete or ReadOnly) block accidental changes or deletion, even for users with Owner rights, until the lock is removed.
questions.af: A padlock on the cash drawer so nobody empties it by mistake.

questions.q: Which service helps govern and protect data across your estate by discovering and classifying it, and supports compliance?
questions.e: Microsoft Purview provides data governance, risk and compliance solutions, including discovering and classifying data.
questions.af: A records officer who catalogues every file and marks which are confidential.

questions.q: How does Azure Policy differ from Azure RBAC?
o: Policy controls what resource configurations are allowed; RBAC controls what users can do
Policy controls who can sign in; RBAC controls pricing
Policy is for storage only; RBAC is for networking only
questions.e: Azure Policy governs resource properties and compliance. RBAC governs which actions identities may perform.
questions.af: Building rules (what a shop may look like) versus staff permissions (who may open the till).

questions.q: A user with the Owner role tries to delete a resource that has a CanNotDelete lock. What happens?
o: The deletion is blocked until the lock is removed
The deletion succeeds because Owners override locks
The resource is moved to another region
questions.e: Locks apply regardless of role. Someone must first remove the lock, which requires the right permission.
questions.af: Even the shop owner has to unlock the safe before taking anything out.

questions.q: Which tool is a web-based graphical interface for creating and managing Azure resources?
questions.e: The Azure portal is the browser-based console for working with Azure resources visually.
questions.af: A shop counter where you point and ask, instead of writing instructions.

questions.q: Which feature gives you an authenticated, browser-based command line with Bash or PowerShell, without installing anything?
questions.e: Cloud Shell runs in the browser and comes with Azure CLI and PowerShell ready to use.
questions.af: Using a cyber café PC that already has all the tools installed.

questions.q: Commands that start with `az`, such as `az group create`, belong to which tool?
questions.e: Azure CLI uses `az` commands and runs on Windows, macOS and Linux. Azure PowerShell uses cmdlets like New-AzResourceGroup.
questions.af: A short command that tells the system what to do, like a USSD code.

questions.q: Defining infrastructure as repeatable templates or scripts instead of clicking in the portal is an example of what?
questions.e: Infrastructure as code deploys consistent environments from declarative or scripted definitions, reducing manual error.
questions.af: A franchise recipe book so every branch makes the same meal.

questions.q: What is Azure Resource Manager (ARM)?
o: The deployment and management layer that processes requests from the portal, CLI, SDKs and templates
questions.e: Every Azure management request goes through ARM. ARM templates (JSON) and Bicep describe resources declaratively.
questions.af: The reception desk every request passes through, whatever door you came in by.

questions.q: Which service lets you manage servers outside Azure (on-premises or other clouds) using the Azure control plane?
questions.e: Azure Arc projects non-Azure servers, Kubernetes clusters and data services into Azure for unified governance.
questions.af: One remote control that works for TVs of different brands.

questions.q: Which tool gives personalised recommendations to improve reliability, security, performance, cost and operational excellence?
questions.e: Azure Advisor analyses your resources and recommends best practices across five pillars.
questions.af: A mentor reviewing your business and suggesting where to cut costs.

questions.q: Which service gives a personalised view of Azure service issues and planned maintenance that affect YOUR resources?
questions.e: Service Health tracks incidents, planned maintenance and health advisories for the services and regions you use.
questions.af: A power company text that tells you about outages in your own neighbourhood.

questions.q: Which service collects, analyses and acts on telemetry from Azure and on-premises environments?
questions.e: Azure Monitor gathers metrics and logs, visualises them, and can trigger alerts and automated actions.
questions.af: A clinic's monitor showing a patient's vital signs and ringing an alarm when they drop.

questions.q: Which Azure Monitor tool lets you write queries to analyse log data?
questions.e: Log Analytics lets you query collected log data using Kusto Query Language (KQL).
questions.af: Searching a till roll for every sale over a certain amount.

questions.q: You want an email when CPU usage on a VM stays above 90 percent for 10 minutes. Which feature do you configure?
questions.e: Azure Monitor alerts notify you or trigger actions when metrics or logs meet conditions you define.
questions.af: A smoke alarm that rings once the smoke level passes a threshold.

questions.q: Which Azure Monitor capability helps you detect performance problems and failures in a live web application?
questions.e: Application Insights is application performance monitoring that tracks requests, failures, dependencies and user behaviour.
questions.af: Watching customer traffic and queues in your shop to spot where people get stuck.

cloud: On-demand delivery of computing services (servers, storage, databases, networking, software) over the internet, usually pay-as-you-go.
opex: CapEx is a big upfront purchase. OpEx is paying as you go for what you use. Cloud shifts spending towards OpEx.
hybrid: Private or on-premises infrastructure combined with a public cloud.
private: Used by one organisation, can be on-premises. The organisation maintains the hardware.
consumption: Pay only for what you use, with no upfront cost.
pricing: Pay-as-you-go suits variable use. Reservations (1 or 3 years) give a discount for steady, predictable use.
serverless: Code runs on demand (Azure Functions). You do not manage servers; billed per execution.
shared: Provider always owns physical datacenter, hosts and network. Customer always owns data, identities and access. The rest depends on IaaS, PaaS or SaaS.
economies: Providers buy and operate at huge scale, so the cost per unit is lower.
elastic: Resources scale out and in automatically with demand.
scale: Horizontal (out) adds more instances. Vertical (up) makes one instance bigger.
sla: A guaranteed uptime target. 99.99% allows less downtime than 99.9%.
reliability: The ability to recover from failures and keep working.
predict: Performance (autoscale, load balancing) and cost (forecasting tools) behave in expected ways.
secgov: Built-in threat protection, policies and compliance offerings. You still configure and govern your own resources.
manage: Management OF the cloud (autoscale, templates, monitoring) and IN the cloud (portal, CLI, APIs).
iaas: You rent VMs, storage and networks and manage the OS, apps and data. Good for lift-and-shift.
paas: Provider manages platform and OS; you manage your app and data (for example App Service).
saas: Finished software you use (Microsoft 365). You manage data, users and access only.
az: Separate datacenters inside one region with independent power, cooling and network.
region: A geographic area with one or more datacenters linked by a low-latency network.
regionpair: Two regions in one geography used for geo-redundancy and disaster recovery.
sovereign: Isolated Azure instances for legal or compliance needs (Azure Government, Azure China).
rg: Logical container for related resources. A resource lives in exactly one.
sub: Billing and access boundary. Management groups above, resource groups below.
mg: Organise subscriptions. Policy and access assigned here are inherited downwards.
container: Lightweight, portable packages that share the host OS kernel.
aks: Managed Kubernetes for running and orchestrating containers.
vm: IaaS compute with full OS control. Use it when you need that control.
vmss: Identical, load-balanced VMs that scale automatically.
avset: Spreads VMs across fault and update domains inside a datacenter.
avd: Desktop and app virtualisation delivered from Azure.
vnet: Your private, isolated network in Azure, divided into subnets.
peering: Connects virtual networks privately over the Microsoft backbone.
expressroute: ExpressRoute: private dedicated connection, not over the internet. VPN Gateway: encrypted tunnel over the internet.
dns: Hosts DNS domains and resolves names using Azure infrastructure.
endpoint: A private IP in your VNet for a service (Private Link). Public endpoints are reachable over the internet.
blob: Object storage for unstructured data like images, video and backups.
files: Managed file shares over SMB or NFS.
redundancy: LRS: one datacenter. ZRS: across zones in a region. GRS: also replicated to a secondary region.
tiers: Hot (frequent), Cool and Cold (infrequent), Archive (rare, offline, hours to rehydrate).
azcopy: AzCopy: command-line copy tool. Storage Explorer: graphical app for Azure Storage.
filesync: Syncs Windows file servers with Azure Files and caches hot files locally.
migrate: Hub to discover, assess and migrate servers, databases and apps.
databox: Physical device to move large amounts of data offline.
entra: Cloud identity service: single sign-on, MFA and access management.
domainsvc: Managed domain join, LDAP and Kerberos/NTLM without running domain controllers.
mfa: Two or more factors: something you know, have or are.
passwordless: Windows Hello for Business, Microsoft Authenticator, FIDO2 security keys.
external: Let guests and partners use their own credentials to access your resources.
conditional: Entra policies that decide access based on location, device and risk.
rbac: Assign roles (Owner, Contributor, Reader) at a scope to grant permissions.
zerotrust: Never trust, always verify. Verify explicitly, least privilege, assume breach.
depth: Layered security: physical, identity, perimeter, network, compute, application, data.
defender: Security posture management and threat protection for Azure and hybrid.
calculator: Estimate the cost of Azure services before you deploy.
costfactors: Resource type, usage, region, bandwidth (inbound free, outbound charged) and offer type.
tags: Name/value pairs to organise resources and report cost by project or team.
budget: Analyse spend and set budgets with alerts.
policy: Rules for resource configuration (for example allowed regions). Audit or deny non-compliant resources.
locks: CanNotDelete or ReadOnly. Apply even to Owners until removed.
purview: Data governance, risk and compliance: discover and classify data across your estate.
cloudshell: Browser-based Bash or PowerShell, already signed in with tools installed.
cli: CLI uses `az` commands. PowerShell uses cmdlets. Both are cross-platform.
iac: Deploy consistent environments from templates or scripts.
arm: Management layer every request goes through. ARM templates (JSON) and Bicep are declarative.
arc: Manage servers and clusters outside Azure from the Azure control plane.
advisor: Recommendations on reliability, security, performance, cost, operational excellence.
servicehealth: Personalised view of incidents and planned maintenance affecting your resources.
monitor: Collects and analyses metrics and logs; alerts and actions.
alerts: Notify or act when metrics or logs meet a condition.
appinsights: Application performance monitoring for live web apps.
